## Obtain raw costs from raw claims data

We use the `usRds` functions `get_IN_REV_costs()`, `get_IN_CLM_costs()` and `get_PS_REV_costs()` to extract Medicare claims with payment amounts for 2006 to 2021, for patients in the matched cohort.

The USRDS claims files hold payments at more than one level [@usrds2025guide]:

- **Institutional claims** (inpatient, outpatient, skilled nursing, home health and hospice) come as a claim file, with one row per claim and the Medicare payment for the whole claim (`CLM_AMT`), and a revenue-center detail file, with one row per revenue center on the claim. `get_IN_CLM_costs()` reads the claim files and `get_IN_REV_costs()` the detail files.
- **Revenue-center lines** carry charges (`REV_CH`) and, for outpatient, home health and hospice claims, a payment (`REVPMT`). Inpatient and skilled nursing lines have no payment field (Appendix B), so inpatient payments come from the claim file only.
- **Claim payments and revenue-center payments describe the same services**, so adding them would count those services twice. For outpatient claims, summed `REVPMT` is about 3% higher than `CLM_AMT` overall [@usrds2025guide].
- **Physician/supplier claims** are read at the line level: `get_PS_REV_costs()` returns each line's payment (`PMTAMT`), with its submitted and allowed charges. Despite the function's name, these are line files, not revenue-center files. In the files available to this project, physician/supplier claims before 2013 come as combined files rather than separate claim and line files, as listed in `usRds`.

The cost outcome uses payment fields (`CLM_AMT`, `REVPMT`, `PMTAMT`), never charges.

#| eval: false

## Merge cost data to cohort

We take the raw claims data and add it to the previously obtained patient cohort data.

This is done as a [nested data frame](https://bookdown.org/Maxine/r4ds/nesting.html) for convenience in subsequent analysis.  A single column is a list, with each element of the list being all cost-related entries for a specific patient.  See [https://bookdown.org/Maxine/r4ds/nesting.html](https://bookdown.org/Maxine/r4ds/nesting.html) for more information on nested data in R.

Patients with no observed claims in a given cost category are assigned empty [tibbles](https://tibble.tidyverse.org/) to ensure consistent downstream processing.

This structure allows costs to be prorated, inflated, and aggregated relative to patient-specific index dates without repeatedly reshaping the data.

While nested data is convenient from many perspectives, it does require the use of the `map()` family of functions from the [`purrr`](https://purrr.tidyverse.org/) package.

#| eval: false

## Costs from start date to end date

We now write code that totals costs for each patient, accounting for the start and finish dates:

- Start: The index date for each patient
- Finish: The earliest of
  - 365 days after the index date (`maximum_followup`)
  - End of Medicare coverage (minimum 1 day)
  - Censoring date for end of data (1/1/2022)

**Current code:** death is not yet an end point of follow-up; it is recorded as the reason follow-up ended only when it falls on one of the dates above ([#10](https://github.com/VagishHemmige/Cryptococcus-cost-analysis/issues/10)). See [End of follow-up](study_costs.qmd#end-of-follow-up).

In addition to total costs, we also calculated total costs grouped by type (Inpatient, Outpatient, Home Health, etc.).

Since claims can span many days, we use the `prorate_costs_by_day()` function from the `usRds` package to divide the costs evenly among the days spanned by
each claim.  Proration is applied before date filtering so that only the portion of each claim overlapping the analytic window contributes to total cost.
